part is rarely the happy-path enqueue/dequeue — it's the interaction of memory reclamation, the C++/Rust memory model,
and the ABA problem under real hardware reordering. Below is a full design, with two concrete algorithms (bounded and
unbounded), the rationale at each decision point, and a validation strategy that actually catches the bugs.

⏺ Lock-Free MPMC Queue in Rust — A Design
A multi-producer/multi-consumer (MPMC) queue is the canonical "looks easy, is brutal" concurrency primitive. The hard
part is rarely the happy-path enqueue/dequeue — it's the interaction of memory reclamation, the C++/Rust memory model,
and the ABA problem under real hardware reordering. Below is a full design, with two concrete algorithms (bounded and
unbounded), the rationale at each decision point, and a validation strategy that actually catches the bugs.

#[derive(Clone)] pub struct Consumer<T> { q: Queue<T> }
impl<T> Producer<T> {
/// Bounded: Err(value) when full. Unbounded: never fails.
pub fn push(&self, value: T) -> Result<(), T>;
impl<T> Consumer<T> {
pub fn pop(&self) -> Option<T>;
Correctness target. Be explicit, because "lock-free" and "linearizable" are different claims:
- Linearizability — every push/pop appears to take effect atomically at some point between its call and return. This
is the property users actually rely on, and the one loom can stress.

This is where "correct but 10× slower than a Mutex" designs come from. Two rules:
3.1 Separate independently-mutated hot atomics onto distinct cache lines. enqueue_pos and dequeue_pos are written by
disjoint sets of threads. If they share a 64-byte line, every producer's CAS invalidates the line in every consumer's
cache and vice versa — pure coherence ping-pong. Pad them:
#[repr(align(128))]                 // not 64 — see §3.3
struct CachePadded<T> { value: T }
Use crossbeam_utils::CachePadded rather than rolling your own.

indices to false-share. For small T, this is a real cost. Options: pad slots (wastes memory, hurts cache density), or
accept it and rely on the ring being large enough that producers and consumers are usually far apart. Measure before

uses 128-byte lines. 64-byte padding leaves you false-sharing on those platforms. crossbeam's CachePadded already
picks the right alignment per target.

and any reclamation epoch counter are worth padding; most everything else should be measured first.

CAS succeeds because the bits match, but A is now a different logical state (e.g., a node that was freed and the
address reused). The CAS-loop's invariant is silently violated.

only ever increases (modulo usize wraparound at 2⁶⁴, irrelevant in practice). There is no "A→B→A" because the position
never returns to a prior value. The per-slot seq stamp uses the full position, including the lap number, so a slot in
lap 2 is distinguishable from the same slot in lap 1. No tagging needed.
5.2 Unbounded queue is exposed. In Michael–Scott, a dequeuer reads head = A, prepares to CAS head to A.next. If A is
dequeued, freed, and a new node is allocated at the same address and becomes head, the stale CAS succeeds with corrupt
results. Classic mitigations:

4. Memory Ordering
The orderings are not decoration — each one is load-bearing. The discipline: an atomic that publishes data uses
Release; the atomic that observes that publication uses Acquire; counters that only gate a subsequent CAS can be
Relaxed.
4.1 Bounded queue.
- slot.seq store after writing the value → Release. It publishes the slot's payload write to the consumer.
- slot.seq load before reading the value → Acquire. It establishes happens-before with the producer's payload write.
This Acquire/Release pair on seq is the synchronization edge that makes the UnsafeCell data access sound.
- enqueue_pos/dequeue_pos CAS → Relaxed is sufficient. These counters hand out tickets; they don't publish payload
data — the seq store/load does. The CAS only needs atomicity, not ordering, because the real data dependency runs
through seq. (Using AcqRel here is a common cargo-cult; it's not wrong, just slower.)
4.2 Unbounded queue.
- Linking a new node: store the node's fields, then CAS tail.next with Release so a consumer that loads next with
Acquire sees the initialized node.
- Reading head/tail/next → Acquire.
- The compare_exchange advancing head/tail → AcqRel on success (it both observes the prior publication and publishes
the advance), Acquire on failure.
4.3 Avoid SeqCst reflexively. SeqCst provides a single total order across all SeqCst operations — you rarely need
that, and on ARM/AArch64 it inserts full barriers (dmb ish) that are markedly more expensive than the ldar/stlr that
Acquire/Release compile to. Reach for SeqCst only when correctness genuinely depends on a total order across multiple
distinct atomic locations (e.g., some flag-based handshakes), and document why.
4.4 Justify every ordering in a comment. A Relaxed with no explanation is indistinguishable from a bug. Future readers
(and your reviewers) cannot re-derive the proof from the code alone.

4.1 Bounded queue.

This Acquire/Release pair on seq is the synchronization edge that makes the UnsafeCell data access sound.
- enqueue_pos/dequeue_pos CAS → Relaxed is sufficient. These counters hand out tickets; they don't publish payload

4.2 Unbounded queue.
- Linking a new node: store the node's fields, then CAS tail.next with Release so a consumer that loads next with
Acquire sees the initialized node.
- Reading head/tail/next → Acquire.

the advance), Acquire on failure.

5. The ABA Problem
ABA: a thread reads a pointer value A, is preempted, and by the time it CASes, the location has gone A → B → A. The
CAS succeeds because the bits match, but A is now a different logical state (e.g., a node that was freed and the
address reused). The CAS-loop's invariant is silently violated.

never returns to a prior value. The per-slot seq stamp uses the full position, including the lap number, so a slot in
lap 2 is distinguishable from the same slot in lap 1. No tagging needed.

results. Classic mitigations:

tag bits mean ABA is improbable, not impossible.

reference it, the address can't be recycled into an ABA, and the problem dissolves. In practice, solving reclamation
solves ABA for free, which is why epoch/hazard schemes are preferred over tag bits in modern Rust.

ABA: a thread reads a pointer value A, is preempted, and by the time it CASes, the location has gone A → B → A. The

reference it, the address can't be recycled into an ABA, and the problem dissolves. In practice, solving reclamation
solves ABA for free, which is why epoch/hazard schemes are preferred over tag bits in modern Rust.

semantics. Note TSan won't see a race that scheduling never triggers — so feed it adversarial workloads.

⏺ A CRDT for Collaborative Text Editing
The honest framing first: text editing is the hardest CRDT to get right, because the data is a totally-ordered
sequence of single characters with no natural keys, edited at fine granularity by people whose intentions ("I'm typing
a word here") are invisible to the merge algorithm. Most of the difficulty is not "does it converge" — almost any
sane design converges — it's "does it converge to something a human would have written." That gap is where
interleaving, anchoring, and tombstones live.
I'll design a list CRDT in the RGA/YATA/Fugue family (the lineage behind Yjs and Automerge), because the
dense-position-identifier family (Logoot/LSEQ) has a fatal interleaving flaw covered in §4.
1. Model and Requirements
The document is a sequence of elements, each one character (or, after optimization, a run — see §8). Every element has
a globally unique, immutable ID and an immutable position in a partial order. The visible text is the in-order
traversal of non-deleted elements.
- Strong eventual consistency (SEC): replicas that have received the same set of operations have identical state,
regardless of delivery order. This is the bar a CRDT must clear and is mechanical to satisfy.

9.5 The layered strategy, in order:
1. Miri on every test — catch UB cheaply and early.
2. Loom on small hand-built models — prove the orderings and the absence of ABA/lost-wakeups exhaustively.
3. TSan on stress tests — validate the real binary on real reorderings.
4. Stress/property tests with conservation invariants — confidence at scale.
5. cargo-careful and ASan/LSan to catch leaks (a stalled-EBR memory leak won't crash but will OOM).
No single tool is sufficient. Loom proves the model; Miri proves no UB; TSan proves the binary; stress tests prove it
scales. Skipping any one of them leaves a class of bug unguarded.
Summary judgment. Default to the bounded Vyukov array queue: it is ABA-immune, allocation-free, needs no reclamation,
gives backpressure, and is the easiest to validate. Reach for the unbounded Michael–Scott (or segmented) queue with
epoch reclamation only when you genuinely cannot bound the queue — and budget accordingly for §6. Pad the two position
counters to 128 bytes, justify every memory ordering in a comment, layer blocking/async on top without touching the
core, batch via bulk reservation and thread-local buffers, and validate with the full loom + Miri + TSan + stress
stack rather than trusting any one of them.

Each element gets an ID (replicaId, counter) — a Lamport-style pair. counter increments per local operation; replicaId

an ID already present is a no-op) and gives concurrent operations a deterministic total tiebreak order.

all do under the hood; representing it as a flat list with origin pointers (§3) is just an optimization of the same

3. Left/Right Anchoring (Origins)
When you insert a character, you must record what it was inserted between so that concurrent inserts at the same spot
can be ordered deterministically and meaningfully. Record both neighbors at insertion time:
Element {
id:          (replicaId, counter),
originLeft:  ElementId | START,   // the element immediately to the left when I typed
originRight: ElementId | END,     // the element immediately to the right when I typed
value:       char,
deleted:     bool,                // tombstone flag, §5
Recording origins by element ID, not index, is the whole game — IDs are stable; indices are not. This is also why
deletion can't physically remove elements: a concurrent insert may name a now-deleted element as its origin, and that
anchor must still resolve (§5).
Why both sides, and the anchor-direction subtlety. A single origin is insufficient to avoid interleaving. Consider the
boundary cases:
- A character typed at the left edge of a region anchors to its right neighbor (there's nothing meaningful on the
left).
- A character typed mid-run anchors left to its predecessor.
The choice of which side a character "belongs to" determines what happens when text is later inserted at the exact
boundary between two concurrent regions. Fugue's key result is that if every element consistently anchors to one side
(forming left-leaning or right-leaning chains), runs of sequential typing form contiguous chains that resist
interleaving. Recording both origins lets the integration algorithm reconstruct these chains; the side preference is
what gives non-interleaving its formal guarantee.

8. Optimization: Block Encoding
Per-character elements are memory- and bandwidth-prohibitive. The decisive optimization (Yjs's core trick): represent
sequential same-author runs as blocks, splitting them lazily only when a concurrent edit lands mid-run. A
10,000-character paste is one block, not 10,000 elements. IDs stay per-character logically ((replicaId,
counter..counter+len)) so anchoring and the algorithms above are unchanged — only the in-memory representation is
compressed. This is what makes these CRDTs competitive with OT on real documents.
9. Validation
Same rigor as any concurrency primitive — convergence bugs are interleaving-dependent and hide easily:
- Property test convergence: generate random concurrent op sequences, apply in every permutation across simulated
replicas, assert identical final state (SEC) and idempotency under redelivery.
- Interleaving regression suite: the "hello"/"world" family and its boundary variants (concurrent inserts at start, at
end, nested) as explicit golden tests — these are the bugs that pass convergence but fail humans.
- Causal-delivery fuzzing: deliver ops in adversarial orders with origins arriving late; assert the pending buffer
integrates correctly and never loses or misplaces an element.
- GC safety tests: simulate a lagging replica and assert no tombstone is collected before the watermark dominates it;
assert post-GC state matches pre-GC visible text.
10. Recommendation
Build a YATA/Fugue-style list CRDT: (replicaId, counter) IDs, both-side origin anchoring, YATA conflict resolution for
convergence-plus-non-interleaving, tombstones for deletion, version vectors for causal delivery and delta sync, block
encoding for size, and watermark-based GC gated on causal stability. Do not roll your own — adopt Yjs or Automerge
unless you have a compelling reason; the conflict-resolution and GC correctness proofs are subtle and these libraries
encode hard-won fixes to anomalies you won't anticipate. Reserve a custom implementation for cases where you need to
embed the CRDT in a constrained runtime or extend it to a non-text structure those libraries don't model.
The one-line summary of the whole design: convergence is easy and nearly automatic; non-interleaving (anchoring) and
garbage collection (membership) are where all the real difficulty concentrates — budget your engineering there.

и нет начальника, кто рассудил бы спор,
лишь правило, простое, как гранит:
сначала origin, потом — кто старше ID.
И буквы не сплетутся в кашу,
твоя строка останется твоей,
моя — моей, и встретятся,
не потеряв ни смысла, ни людей.
А мёртвое — не трогаем, пока
последний, самый медленный из нас
не подтвердит: я видел, я согласен.

рвутся к одной ячейке памяти,
и кто-то проиграет CAS,
но проигравший — не умрёт:
он развернётся и пойдёт по кругу снова,
пока хоть кто-то движется вперёд.
Так и мы — пишем порознь, врозь,
ты — «привет», я — «здравствуй» в тот же миг,
и нет начальника, кто рассудил бы спор,
лишь правило, простое, как гранит:
сначала origin, потом — кто старше ID.
И буквы не сплетутся в кашу,
твоя строка останется твоей,
моя — моей, и встретятся,
не потеряв ни смысла, ни людей.
А мёртвое — не трогаем, пока
последний, самый медленный из нас
не подтвердит: я видел, я согласен.
И только в этот тихий общий час
надгробья падают, и память дышит,
и дерево становится — строкой.
Если хочешь — могу в другом настроении: без технической метафоры, или построже по форме (сонет, верлибр), или вообще
на английском. 🙂

он развернётся и пойдёт по кругу снова,
пока хоть кто-то движется вперёд.
Так и мы — пишем порознь, врозь,
ты — «привет», я — «здравствуй» в тот же миг,
и нет начальника, кто рассудил бы спор,
лишь правило, простое, как гранит:
сначала origin, потом — кто старше ID.
И буквы не сплетутся в кашу,
твоя строка останется твоей,
моя — моей, и встретятся,
не потеряв ни смысла, ни людей.
А мёртвое — не трогаем, пока
последний, самый медленный из нас
не подтвердит: я видел, я согласен.
И только в этот тихий общий час
надгробья падают, и память дышит,
и дерево становится — строкой.
Если хочешь — могу в другом настроении: без технической метафоры, или построже по форме (сонет, верлибр), или вообще
на английском. 🙂

Acquire/Release ordering discipline (with Relaxed for ticket counters and avoiding reflexive SeqCst), blocking/async
wrappers via spin→yield→park escalation, batching through bulk slot reservation and thread-local buffers, and
validation with loom + Miri + TSan + stress tests; second, a CRDT for collaborative text editing in the RGA/YATA/Fugue
family — unique (replicaId, counter) IDs, left/right origin anchoring to avoid the character-level interleaving
anomaly, unavoidable tombstones for deletion, causal delivery and delta-sync via version vectors, and garbage
collection gated on causal stability (with the membership/offline-replica tension as the real hard part), plus block
encoding as the key size optimization. We closed with some light conversation and a poem tying those themes together.
